extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / literate early-18th-century public interested in taste, theatre, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and letters offering evaluative principles for writing, acting, taste, and public conduct (especially comedy and theatre) aimed at improving public manners and artistic quality. Mixes concrete examples, anti-patterns, and moral/political reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive circumstantiality / verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticises 'this odd turn of Head which can play away its Words, with uttering nothing to the Purpose' — the habit of being very circumstantial and careful to be exact that wastes others' time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalty: when a speaker/writer digresses into needless detail (geography of a jest, birth and parentage of a person mentioned) or delays the point (saying one will 'enter into the matter' then elaborating at length). Example/anti-pattern: the man who begins to 'settle the Geography of the Jest' and proceeds without arriving at the point. Prefer brief, purposeful expression; value readers' or listeners' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-rely on authorities; trust your own judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects to those who buttress every point with learned citations (e.g. 'According to that excellent Divine... in the fifteenth Sermon... With the Pious and Learned Dr. Beveridge...') instead of simply addressing the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: a preacher who reads too much and 'was so Humble that he did not trust enough to his own Parts.' Guidance: use authorities sparingly and only when necessary; avoid turning a talk into a parade of citations that dilute the speaker's own argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid frivolous disputation (don't raise needless doubts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemns people who 'are ever labouring to raise Arguments with you about Matters you will give up to them without the least Controversy' and who can 'put you to prove that Snow is white.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: disputants who transform small knowledge into a capacity of raising doubts, who are 'always frivolous and always unanswerable.' Guidance: avoid argument for its own sake; do not force interlocutors to defend obvious facts or engage in hair-splitting that serves no constructive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer just, proper, and natural writing to forced 'point' or antiquarian affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of imitators who mistake Milton's excellence for uncouth or antique words, or who imitate 'Point, or Turn' (as in Cowley) so that 'what is Just, Proper and Natural does not seem to be the Question.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: value naturalness and propriety over quaintness or forced antithesis; avoid making a 'quaint Antithesis' the aim, or producing forced allusion to create a 'turn.' Anti-pattern: authors who are 'too Witty' in the bad sense—fine instead of graceful—and who borrow the worst traits of admired authors as mere mannerisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting must be exact and graceful; small failures are contemptible
rubrics_metrics.description: In theatrical speaking, 'if the Performer is not exactly proper and graceful, he is utterly ridiculous... to be the least out is contemptible.' Performing the part is not enough; precision and grace are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring guidance: where the expected pleasure derives from ear and eye alone, even minor defects reduce or destroy the effect. Anti-patterns: hoarseness, awkwardness, or slovenly delivery in performers who rely on the weight of subject-matter elsewhere (preachers/pleaders may be excused; actors are not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep physical spectacle (acrobatics, tumbling) separate from intellectual acting
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes between corporeal actors (rope-dancers, tumblers) who serve an audience 'who have no Faculty above Eyesight' and intellectual actors who represent the passions of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production guidance: dismiss bodily actors to places like the Bear-Garden; do not mix stunt-based entertainment with performances that require subtlety of speech and character. Anti-pattern: plays that conflate tumbling and rope-dancing with the art of theatrical representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject-matter to genre; avoid horrific or sordid material in comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues that incantations, sacrifices, and ceremonies of Devil-worship are appropriate to tragedy (e.g., Macbeth) where horror is fitting, but 'extremely foreign' to comedy and cannot be made entertaining except by a genius like Shakespeare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: choose machinery and subject so they suit the tone: dark, bloody, or horrid matter belongs to tragic machines; comedy should avoid disagreeable or shocking scenes that cannot be transformed by high imagination. Anti-pattern: comedies that include black-lamb sacrifices or devil worship merely for sensation (example: Shadwell's Lancashire Witches criticized here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indecent or vulgar jests; don't sacrifice the best audience to the lowest taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects to 'Passages, which... raise the loudest Mirth, though they are painful to right Sense, and an Outrage upon Modesty'—authors who 'sacrifice the best Part of his Audience to the worst' or 'write to the Orange-Wenches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial/aesthetic rule: aim to please people of 'the best Understanding' and preserve modesty in representation. Anti-patterns: relying on gross, indelicate jokes to get laughter at the expense of decent taste and the more respectable audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test of civic/political glory (Tully): love, confidence, and deserved honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes Tully: 'The Perfection of Glory... consists in these three Particulars: That the People love us; that they have Confidence in us; that being affected with a certain Admiration towards us, they think we deserve Honour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application guidance: use these three criteria to distinguish solid, lasting glory (as in Peter the Great's reforms) from empty ostentation (as ascribed to Louis XIV's court). Consider whether fame comes from virtue or from vain display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consummate (court) glory requires the prince's favour and popular affection
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds to Tully's civic test that under a monarchical constitution 'Riches, Power, Honour, Command and Glory should have no Charms, but as accompanied with the Affection of his Prince'—a favourite should be popular because a favourite and a favourite because popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political/aesthetic implication: for an individual's glory at court to be stable and honourable, it must rest on genuine affection and not merely on accumulation of external marks (riches, titles). Anti-pattern: glory that depends solely on opulence, equipage, or ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: True love is shown by actions, constancy, and presence (not mere professions)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Lydia Novell's letter: a pretender 'is always talking of Constancy, but vouchsafes to visit me but once a Fortnight... When he leaves the Town he writes once in six Weeks... He has the Cant of an impatient Lover, but keeps the Pace of a Lukewarm one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation guidance: do not take professions alone as evidence of affection; prefer demonstrated constancy through visits, attentions, and timely communications. Anti-pattern: rhetorical professions of torment and ecstasy with no corresponding acts.
